 Son Suk-ku puts the badge back on for Netflix's 'The Blue Road.' This time, he digs deeper
 Published : Nov. 18, 2026 - 11:30:19
 Add The Korea Herald on Google
 Link copied!
 Lee Yoon-seo 
Covering TV, streaming, esports and the business and cultural trends shaping Korean entertainment
 Subscribe + 
 Actor shares how his fourth turn as a detective became a creative breakthrough
 Eita Nagayama (left) and Son Suk-ku pose for a photo during a press conference in Seoul, Tuesday. (Yonhap) Put a badge and a heavy burden on actor Son Suk-ku, and streaming hits inevitably follow.
 Having cemented his status as a global K-drama powerhouse through dogged detective roles in "A Killer Paradox" and "Big Bet," the 43-year-old screen mainstay is returning to television fresh off Disney+’s mystery series "Nine Puzzles."
 Now, he is doubling down on the genre for Netflix’s new murder mystery "The Blue Road," starring opposite Japanese A-lister Eita Nagayama.
 A moody adaptation of a cult-classic 2002 Japanese-Korean manga, "The Blue Road" tracks Korean detective Kim Seok (Son) and his Japanese counterpart Inose Hiroshi (Nagayama) as they join forces to untangle a string of grisly, cross-border serial murders.
 The role marks Son’s fourth turn as a detective in his late-blooming, 10-year career. Fueled by crime blockbusters like "The Roundup" and soulful human dramas such as "My Liberation Notes," Son's trajectory has turned him into a rare double threat: the defining face of Korean crime dramas and a national heartthrob.
 Yet while the premise of the series echoes his past work, the actor emphasized that he took the part because it breaks the conventional detective mold, prioritizing an internal reckoning over police work.
 "What drew me to Kim Seok was that, beyond his appeal as a professional detective, he is someone seeking something deeper on a personal level," Son said during a press conference in Seoul on Tuesday.
 "That deeply human aspect of the character appealed to me."
 For Son, the series also arrived at a pivotal moment in his career. Having hit a creative plateau, he viewed teaming up with director Han Jun-hee as an essential catalyst to push his craft forward.
 "By the time I came across 'The Blue Road,' I felt I had reached a ceiling as an actor. (Actors) are not athletes, so we don't have records to measure ourselves against, but it felt like being unable to break the 13-second mark in the 100-meter dash," he said.
 "I thought that meeting the director for 'The Blue Road' might help me break through that barrier and move on to the next stage."
 The next stage involved overhauling his physical and vocal toolkit, with Son changing his appearance and speech patterns in ways he had previously shied away from.
 "I went places I had hesitated to go before, or simply never felt the need to venture into," he said.
 Sharing the screen with Son is Nagayama, a decorated Japanese screen veteran with a 25-year resume, widely recognized for megahits like "Nodame Cantabile."
 For Nagayama, signing onto the cross-border production came down to director Han’s deep passion for Japanese cinema and an artistic kinship with his co-star.
 "Director Han told me, 'Among Korean directors, no one knows and loves Japanese films and dramas as much as I do.' He also told me that I was the only person he could imagine playing Inose. I was genuinely happy to hear that," Nagayama said.
 "I was also already a fan of Son Suk-ku's films and dramas, so I was quite nervous. But as soon as we met, I felt that we shared the same sensibility."
 For Han, it was the unique marriage of hard-boiled noir and the source material's exploration of historical friction between Japan and Korea that inspired him to bring the story to life more than two decades after its print debut.
 "I read the original manga about 20 years ago. It had a grotesque appeal, but there was also a sadness running through it that made me feel it could tell a multifaceted story," Han said.
 "The drama features detectives, criminals and other characters. I thought that bringing all of this together within a genre framework could make for a series with a variety of compelling dimensions."
 Rather than spelling out the series’ central themes, other cast members hinted at a narrative that transcends the standard whodunit.
 "The script tells a small story that is also a big story, and a big story that is also a small one," said Kim Shin-rok ("Hellbound"), who portrays Lee Yun-ok, an enigmatic Zainichi Korean businesswoman.
 As the cast prepares to unveil the layered narrative, Nagayama made clear whose reaction he is watching most closely.
 "I hope many people watch the series, but I especially hope Korean audiences will embrace it," he said.
 "The Blue Road" drops globally on Netflix this Friday.
 Eita Nagayama (left) and Son Suk-ku pose for a photo during a press conference in Seoul, Tuesday. (Yonhap)
